title: Worship & Christian Practice
plainLanguageTitle: How Christians worship and practice their faith

sources.workingBank: WCP — Dividing Doctrines — Worship & Christian Practice (Working Bank) v1

sections.title: Regulative and Normative Principles

questions.prompt: What determines which practices are acceptable in a Christian worship service?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only practices commanded by God in Scripture, explicitly or by necessary implication, may be included as elements of worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Practices are permissible unless Scripture forbids them, provided they are consistent with biblical teaching.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Worship should follow the authoritative liturgical tradition received and preserved by the Church.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scripture establishes the essential purposes of worship, while the Church exercises contextual and pastoral discernment over its forms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What establishes sufficient biblical warrant for an element of worship?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-01 = A

choices.label: A
choices.text: Explicit biblical commands.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biblical commands together with binding apostolic examples and necessary implications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The broader pattern of worship throughout Scripture, insofar as it remains applicable under the New Covenant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Should Christians distinguish between the elements of worship and their circumstances?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Only biblically warranted elements are permissible; churches may exercise judgment concerning circumstances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, but the distinction is not always clear enough to function as a strict rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No strict distinction is necessary; all worship decisions should be evaluated according to biblical principles and edification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

helpText: An element is an act of worship, such as prayer or singing. A circumstance concerns how an act is arranged, such as its time or location.

questions.prompt: What authority does a church have to require worship practices not explicitly commanded in Scripture?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A church may regulate circumstances but may not introduce or require additional elements of worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A church may establish appropriate practices for order and unity, but should not treat them as divine commands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A church may authoritatively prescribe rites and ceremonies within its received ecclesiastical tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Such practices should ordinarily remain matters of local discretion or individual Christian liberty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

editorialNotes: The governing principle and a proposed application are separate judgments.

sections.title: Liturgy and Worship Forms

questions.prompt: What form should a regular Christian worship service ordinarily take?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historically received and authoritative liturgy with prescribed prayers, readings, and rites.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recognizable liturgical structure that preserves historic practices while allowing adaptation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An orderly but flexible service organized around Scripture, prayer, praise, and preaching.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A substantially spontaneous service that permits the congregation and its leaders to respond freely during worship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No single worship structure should be normative for all churches.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Why should historic liturgical forms be retained?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-04 = A or B

choices.label: A
choices.text: They belong to the Church's authoritative and received tradition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They preserve theological continuity and protect worship from error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They provide valuable order and spiritual formation, but may be substantially revised.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Which elements should be present in every ordinary principal weekly worship service?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Public reading of Scripture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preaching or exposition of Scripture.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Corporate prayer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Congregational singing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Celebration of the Lord's Supper or Eucharist.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Confession of faith or recitation of a creed.

choices.label: G
choices.text: A formal blessing or benediction.

choices.label: H
choices.text: No individual element on this list must occur at every such gathering.

choices.label: I
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What kinds of songs are appropriate for congregational worship?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the biblical Psalms should be sung.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only inspired biblical songs, including Psalms and other scriptural canticles, should be sung.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs are appropriate when their teaching is faithful to Scripture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A broad range of Christian songs is appropriate, including those emphasizing personal experience and devotion rather than explicit doctrinal teaching, provided they do not contradict the faith.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: How strictly should song lyrics be evaluated for theological precision?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-06 = C or D

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every theological claim should be carefully consistent with the church's doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Songs should be biblically sound in substance, with reasonable allowance for poetic expression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Songs may employ broad, experiential, or poetic language without satisfying the precision expected of doctrinal teaching.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What role should musical instruments have in corporate worship?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Instruments should not accompany congregational worship because they lack sufficient New Covenant warrant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Instruments are permissible but not required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Instruments should ordinarily be included as a fitting expression of praise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Instruments should generally be avoided for reasons of simplicity, reverence, or congregational participation, although they are not inherently forbidden.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Should churches observe recurring Christian festivals and seasons, such as Christmas, Easter, Advent, and Lent?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Churches should not institute additional recurring holy days as acts of corporate religious observance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Such observances are permissible and beneficial, but should remain optional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historic Christian calendar should ordinarily shape the church's worship and spiritual life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A church may establish certain feasts and seasons as obligatory observances for its members, even when those observances are not individually commanded in Scripture.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What should occupy the central place in the regular gathered worship of the Church?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reading and preaching of God's Word.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Word and the Lord's Supper or Eucharist as complementary centers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Eucharistic liturgy as the central act of the Church's corporate worship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prayer, praise, teaching, and other acts of worship without one necessarily taking precedence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Are dramatic presentations or choreographed dance appropriate within a Christian worship service?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. Such presentations should not be introduced as elements of worship without biblical warrant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They may occasionally serve as illustrations or teaching aids, but should not ordinarily be treated as acts of worship.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are legitimate forms of worship when conducted reverently and for the congregation's edification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their suitability depends on the specific form, context, and purpose rather than a universal rule.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

editorialNotes: At WCP-77.5, retain the wording “A church may establish” wherever it occurs. The authority claim should leave room for traditions that locate it in a particular church.

sections.title: Sabbath and Lord's Day

questions.prompt: How does the biblical Sabbath command apply to Christians under the New Covenant?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Sabbath command remains binding, and the seventh day (Saturday) is still the appointed day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Sabbath command remains binding, but the Christian Sabbath is now observed on the first day (Sunday).

choices.label: C
choices.text: The principle of setting aside one day in seven remains binding, but the particular day is not universally fixed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ; Sunday is specially appointed for Christian worship, but is not a continuation of the Jewish Sabbath command.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and Christians are not obligated to sanctify a particular day, although regular worship remains important.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What activities should ordinarily be avoided on the Sabbath?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-11 = A, B, or C

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ordinary employment, unnecessary commerce, and ordinary recreation, except for works of necessity and mercy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ordinary work and commerce, while allowing recreation compatible with rest and worship.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activities that prevent worship and meaningful rest, with considerable individual discretion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What status should Sunday worship have?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-11 = D or E

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sunday is the appointed Christian day for regular corporate worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sunday follows a strong apostolic precedent and should ordinarily be preferred, but is not universally required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Christians should gather regularly, but no particular weekday is appointed by God.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: To what extent is regular corporate worship obligatory for Christians?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Christians are ordinarily obligated to gather for worship every week unless providentially prevented.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate worship is a Christian duty, but Scripture does not establish a universally binding weekly frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Corporate worship is strongly encouraged, but attendance frequency is principally a matter of individual conscience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Christians may faithfully practice their faith without regular organized corporate worship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: How should churches treat members who differ over Sabbath or Lord's Day observance?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The church should teach and uphold a specific Sabbath obligation as binding on its members.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The church should maintain a common day of worship while permitting disagreement over restrictions on work and recreation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The church should permit substantial liberty concerning both observance and the day itself, while encouraging regular assembly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

editorialNotes: Distinguish the day on which Christians assemble from whether a Sabbath command continues.

sections.title: Prayer and Intercession

questions.prompt: To whom may Christian prayer properly be addressed?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prayer should be addressed to God the Father, through Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prayer should ordinarily be addressed to the Father, but direct prayer to Jesus Christ or the Holy Spirit is also appropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prayer may be addressed directly to any Person of the Trinity without a prescribed preference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

helpText: This concerns direct prayer to God. Requests for saintly intercession are addressed separately.

questions.prompt: May Christians request the intercession of departed saints?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. Christians should direct their prayers to God and may request intercession from living believers, but not address the departed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Departed believers may intercede for the Church in heaven, but Christians should not address requests to them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes. Christians may request the intercession of departed saints, distinguishing such requests from the worship due to God alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: How important should the invocation of saints be in Christian devotional life?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-15 = C

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is permissible, but entirely optional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a valuable and encouraged expression of communion with the saints.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an established and integral practice within the Church's devotional and liturgical tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Should Christians pray for people who have died?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Such prayers may benefit the departed, including those undergoing purification after death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. Christians should ask God to grant the departed mercy, rest, and blessedness without necessarily defining how those prayers operate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Christians may commend the departed to God's mercy, but should not assume that prayer changes their eternal condition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No. Prayer for the dead is not warranted by Scripture and should not be practiced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What relationship should established written prayers and spontaneous prayers have in Christian worship?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Established liturgical prayers should be the ordinary foundation of public worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Written prayers and spontaneous prayers are both appropriate and should complement one another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spontaneous prayer should generally be preferred, although written prayers are permissible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous prayer alone should ordinarily be used, rather than prescribed prayer texts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Is fasting an expected practice for Christians today?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Christians are obligated to observe prescribed fasting disciplines or seasons established by the Church.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. Fasting is an expected Christian discipline, although its timing and frequency may vary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fasting is spiritually beneficial, but entirely voluntary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fasting may be practiced, but it carries no particular New Covenant expectation or spiritual importance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Should churches organize or prescribe periods of corporate fasting?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-18 = B or C

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Churches should regularly call their members to shared fasting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, on particular occasions of prayer, repentance, or discernment, without establishing a universally binding calendar.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Churches may encourage fasting, but participation and timing should remain matters of individual conscience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

editorialNotes: Distinguish intercession, invocation, prayers for the departed, and fasting.

sections.title: Images, Icons, and Veneration

questions.prompt: Is it permissible to create visual depictions of Jesus Christ?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. Depicting Christ violates the prohibition against making images of God.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. Images of Christ may be used for education, historical representation, or art, but should not receive religious veneration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes. Images of Christ may be used devotionally and may receive appropriate veneration directed to the person represented rather than the material image.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What role may images of Christ have in gathered worship?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  WCP-19 = B or C

choices.label: A
choices.text: They may be displayed as art or instruction, but should not function as devotional aids.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They may serve as devotional aids that direct attention toward Christ, without receiving veneration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They may be venerated as holy icons, with honor directed toward Christ rather than the object itself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Although depictions of Christ are permissible elsewhere, they should not be used in corporate worship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Is it permissible to represent God the Father visually?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. God the Father should not be visually depicted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Symbolic imagery may refer to the Father, but artistic depictions purporting to portray his person are inappropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Figurative artistic representations are permissible if understood as symbolic rather than literal portraits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Such imagery may appropriately appear in Christian devotional or liturgical settings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: What role may images of angels, Mary, and other saints have in Christian religious settings?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Representations of these figures should not be used as religious images.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They may be displayed for historical remembrance, decoration, or instruction, but not venerated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They may serve as devotional aids directing attention to exemplary figures in the faith, without receiving religious veneration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They may receive appropriate religious veneration, distinct from the worship reserved for God.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: How should acts such as bowing before, kissing, or offering incense to sacred images be understood?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Such acts constitute prohibited religious devotion to images.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are inappropriate practices, although the intent of the worshiper means they do not necessarily constitute idolatry in every instance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They can be legitimate expressions of honor directed toward the person represented, rather than the physical object.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are proper and established expressions of veneration within the Church's received liturgical tradition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Are crosses and crucifixes appropriate for display in churches?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neither crosses nor crucifixes should serve as religious images or symbols in corporate worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A simple cross is appropriate, but a crucifix depicting Christ is not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both crosses and crucifixes are appropriate visual reminders of Christ's sacrifice, but neither should receive religious veneration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both are appropriate and may receive reverent honor within the Church's devotional tradition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure.

questions.prompt: Should relics or physical objects associated with saints have a role in Christian devotion?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: They should not be objects of religious honor or devotional practice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They may be preserved as historical reminders, but should not receive religious veneration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They may be appropriately honored or venerated in connection with the saints and God's work through them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure.

editorialNotes: Keep the permissibility of making an image separate from its devotional use or veneration.

Question IDs, answer choices, and existing review flags follow the current Friend Feedback edition. Use the dimension headings to enter any topic. For a guided reading, continue to the next main question after each applicable branch.

An opening question starts its topic. A common follow-up is available to all readers of that topic. Conditional follow-ups use the answer letters shown. Optional depth is by choice, and uncertainty alone never triggers a doctrinal inference.

vocabulary.definition: The view that acts of gathered worship require authorization from Scripture, explicitly or by necessary implication.
The view that churches may choose practices for gathered worship within the limits of scriptural prohibitions and biblical teaching.
The acts that constitute worship, such as prayer, Scripture reading, preaching, and singing.
Practical arrangements for carrying out acts of worship, such as the time and place of a service.
The ordered form of a community’s public worship, or in some traditions the name of a particular service.
Sunday as the day associated with Christ’s resurrection and Christian gathering for worship.
Prayer offered on behalf of someone else.
Addressing a departed saint to request their prayer or intercession.
A sacred image, especially a depiction of Christ, a saint, or a biblical event in Eastern Christian practice.
Religious honor shown to a saint, sacred image, or relic, distinguished by traditions that practice it from the worship due to God alone.
A saint’s bodily remains or an object closely associated with a saint, kept for remembrance or devotion.
